products.name: Candy Crush
products.key_insight: Candy Crush Saga has generated over $20 billion in lifetime revenue by perfecting a single behavioral loop: give players a sense of near-mastery, then introduce failure through randomness, then offer to sell the solution. This is not accidental — it's the direct application of Natasha Schull's 'machine zone' concept from casino design to mobile gaming. The game's levels are algorithmically tuned to produce a specific failure rate: too easy and players don't spend, too hard and they quit. The optimal frustration point — where players believe they 'almost had it' and one more try (or one purchased power-up) will succeed — is the core monetization engine. The lives system (5 lives, 30-minute regeneration) creates artificial scarcity of play itself, making continued play feel like a premium commodity. King's brilliance is making the monetization feel like the player's choice ('I choose to buy a power-up') rather than the system's design ('the level was tuned to make you fail without one'). Candy Crush is the purest distillation of free-to-play behavioral economics: the product is free, and frustration is the revenue model.
products.top_technique: Near-Miss Level Design as Monetization Engine
